Photograph: Athit Perawongmetha/Reuters Opinion Grand Theft Auto VI Did you come down with GTA flu? I won’t judge – I may even join you in Vice City
 Imogen West-Knights Millions are throwing sickies and no wonder. For gamers who have waited 13 years, this is the equivalent of a football World Cup
 Sat 21 Nov 2026 03.00 EST Last modified on Sat 21 Nov 2026 12.22 EST Share I f there were an unusual number of people missing from your workplace at the back end of this week, they may have come down with GTA flu . You don’t need to be a video game person to have heard that there’s a new instalment of Grand Theft Auto , the enormously popular series in which you drive around sprawling American cities committing crimes. It has been all over the news. And if you are not a video game person, maybe that seems baffling. Why is this game such a big deal?
 Let me assure you that this is no ordinary video game release. The last GTA instalment, GTA V, came out in 2013, so fans have waited 13 years for this game. On Wednesday, before the game had even been released in the US, PlayStation Network experienced widespread disruption attributed to an overload of people trying to download an update needed for the game. After its first day of sales, it was already thought to be the biggest entertainment launch of all time, having made $2.36bn (£1.8bn) – nearly as much as the latest Spider-Man film over its entire run.
 In terms of the sheer number of people excited about it, it’s a cultural moment that might rank alongside something like a football World Cup. And so it has spawned something being called the GTA flu: millions of people around the world pulled sickies in order to devote the day of release to cracking incalculable numbers of beers and playing until their eyes go funny. This isn’t the first time GTA flu has swept the world: it happened back in 2013 for GTA V’s release, too. There is, alas, still no cure.
 I asked around, and plenty of my friends and acquaintances admitted to being among the GTA bunkers, although most had booked the day off rather than feigning a cough to get their gaming hours in. One friend reported that every single man on her team had requested leave on Thursday, and I heard about another person who went a step further and timed quitting his job in order for his unemployment to coincide with this momentous week. On Thursday, I went to visit a friend, a man who had booked annual leave weeks in advance for the release of GTA VI, to see what the fuss was about.
 View image in fullscreen A fan shows off his copy of Grand Theft Auto VI at a launch party for the game, New York, 19 November 2026. Photograph: David ’Dee’ Delgado/AP When I arrived, he was at a quayside bar called the Rusty Anchor, losing a game of pool to a man in wraparound shades. We spent an hour or so driving around so he could give me a sense of the world he was just starting to discover – gorgeously rendered sunsets over the sea, rundown liquor stores and truck stops fringed with Florida-esque plantlife creeping through the concrete. The map for this game is huge – twice as big as it was in the last instalment and nearly as big as the real city of Miami – and getting to know all its corners will involve many, many hours of adventuring for its players.
 Something else caught my eye in the news reports about GTA mania, though. I came across a post on a website describing an event being planned by players of GTA V, the 2013 instalment. Gamers would gather inside the online, collaborative version of the game and take a final, ceremonial drive through the game’s city, Los Santos. No reckless driving, no running down pedestrians, just a stately procession to say farewell to the world they had loved, before embarking on GTA VI. They were calling this “the last ride”.

 We made GTA 6, the world’s biggest video game – we should have working conditions to match | Nestor Uriarte Read more I was never a GTA person. Not for any moral handwringing reasons (and look, yes, this is a game where you can and do kill people), but just because I was always more drawn to colourful platform games in my youth, or glorious time-sinks such as The Sims . But I am very much an open-world video game person. The rolling grasslands of Red Dead Redemption 2 , the twinkling forests of The Legend of Zelda games, the bamboo groves of Ghost of Tsushima : all of these are places I have spent a lot of my life. Several times in any given week I think longingly about Zelda’s Kingdom of Hyrule in particular, knowing that I can just boot up the game and go there, but now that I’ve finished the main story, and practically all of the side adventures, it feels like a place I can’t quite go back to.
 I miss it there. Anywhere you spend a lot of time accrues meaning, and modern video games create vast, richly detailed places to become attached to. That last ride through Los Santos makes sense to me. What my friend who I played some GTA with on Thursday was excited about mostly wasn’t firing a gun, or driving a really sick whip. It was getting to know the world.
 It might seem sort of silly for people to get excited enough about a video game to risk pissing off their employers by pretending to be sick. I wouldn’t say that I approve , necessarily, of people bunking off school and work. Certainly not in a national newspaper. But I do understand. For millions of players, this week is their first introduction to a world where they will spend hours upon hours, exploring, marvelling, discovering. And, yes, sometimes shooting drug dealers.
 Imogen West-Knights is a writer and journalist
